title: Sandhi
scope: A complete guided chapter for reading common Classical Sanskrit sandhi. Specialist Vedic recitation and the full Pāṇinian derivation system need separate chapters.
schema: Each card: title, separated Devanagari, joined Devanagari, IAST, boundary rule, teaching text, optional depth.

lessons.title: Where words meet
lessons.goal: Find the sounds at a boundary before choosing a rule.
cards: This means ‘Rama is here / exists’. Joining changes the sounds where the words meet. The meaning and grammatical identity of the words remain. By the end of this chapter, you will explain the change and recover the two words.
Sandhi means joining. Our examples use Classical Sanskrit. An isolated teaching pair is not necessarily a complete sentence; the full reading at the end is.
Look at Sita’s final ā and api’s initial a. Those two vowels meet. Most of each word stays unchanged. Start with this small boundary, rather than trying to memorise the whole joined expression.
The plus sign marks the original word boundary. It is an explanation device, not part of ordinary Sanskrit spelling. This example means ‘Sita too’.
A vowel sign is still a vowel.
In सीता, the ा sign supplies the final ā. You do not need to see a separate आ letter to have a vowel boundary. Read sounds first, then inspect how Devanagari writes them.
A consonant without a vowel sign normally includes a. Virāma removes that inherent vowel: त is ta, त् is t. Sandhi is not a rule about adjoining printed shapes.
Three families give you a map.
ā + a · t + a · ḥ + a

A vowel ending leads you to vowel sandhi. A consonant ending leads you to consonant sandhi. A visarga ending needs its own checks, including the vowel before it. First identify the family; learn its cases one at a time.

Visarga is a consonantal sound, but teaching it separately prevents a large and confusing consonant table. The visarga result depends on the ending, so this map intentionally gives no universal ḥ + a answer.
अ / आ · इ / ई · उ / ऊ
a / ā · i / ī · u / ū

The line over ā, ī or ū marks a long vowel. Sandhi may treat both lengths as one family, while other rules depend on a specific length. Keep that distinction visible; ‘a vowel’ is sometimes too broad a description.
Also recognise ṛ, ṝ and rare ḷ. Sanskrit e, ai, o and au are long vowels. Roman th, dh, kh and similar pairs each represent one aspirated consonant.
At a real pause, read the pause form. In continuous speech, inspect the following sound. Do not force a rule across every full stop simply because two written words happen to be neighbours.
External sandhi is characteristic of continuous Sanskrit, but pedagogical separation, pause and textual conventions matter. A space alone does not guarantee a spoken pause.
Inside a word is another setting.

Sandhi also helps form words. Here a stem and a case ending combine to mean ‘by the winds’. Keep internal formation separate from joining already formed words; similar sounds do not always receive identical treatment.
Some endings receive treatment resembling external or pada sandhi. Morphology supplies the input form; joining rules alone cannot construct every Sanskrit word.

For each example, name the final sound, the next initial sound, and the setting. Then ask what changes and why. This small routine will carry you through vowels, stops, nasals and visarga without one enormous rule chart.
Prerequisites: recognise Devanagari or IAST sounds and basic word forms. If vowel signs or final consonants are unfamiliar, complete that sound lesson before continuing.

lessons.title: Two vowels of one family
lessons.goal: Apply savarṇa-dīrgha across all ordinary short/long combinations.
cards: Sita ends in ā. Api begins in a. These are two lengths of the same vowel family. At this ordinary vowel boundary, they merge into one long ā. Sītāpi means ‘Sita too’.
The traditional name is savarṇa-dīrgha: similar vowels combine as a long vowel. Protected vowels and special settings will come later.
Read sī-tā-pi. The boundary no longer has two vowel syllables. The long ā is one vowel, not ā followed by an invisible a. This helps you read the word and later count syllables in verse.
The joined expression retains the grammatical words sītā and api. A phonetic merger does not turn them into a compound.
A long ā meeting short a produces long ā. It does not create an extra-long vowel. The rule gives the family’s long vowel whether either input is short or long.
Pluta, a specially prolonged vowel, is a separate category. Do not infer pluta by adding ordinary vowel lengths together.
अ + अ · अ + आ · आ + अ · आ + आ
Short plus short, short plus long, long plus short, and long plus long all give ā. For a real word example, deva + ālaya becomes devālaya: ‘a dwelling of a deity’, a temple.
Savarṇa concerns sound class, not identical printed letters. Compound formation supplies the words deva and ālaya; sandhi supplies the joining.
Ati ends in short i; iva begins in short i. The result is atīva, ‘exceedingly’. The same family rule applies if one or both meeting i vowels are long. All four combinations give ī.
Another useful formation is adhi + īśvara → adhīśvara, ‘overlord’. The rule is about adjacent boundary vowels, not every i anywhere in a word.
Su means ‘well’; uktam means ‘said’. Together they form sūktam, ‘well said’ or a hymn. Two short u vowels become one long ū. Mixing short and long u at this boundary also gives ū.
su + ū… , sū + u… and sū + ū… all have the same boundary result ū under the ordinary rule. The example is a formed expression, not a claim that su is a freely inflecting noun.

The traditional vowel family includes ṛ and ṝ. Their ordinary like-vowel combination is represented as ṝ, but actual examples are extremely rare. Learn to recognise the row; spend your reading practice on a, i and u first.

Whitney notes that practical occurrence is questionable. Traditional savarṇa treatment also connects ṛ and ḷ; rare mixed vocalic-r/l cases require a detailed grammar. Do not invent everyday vocabulary to make a rare rule look common.
The result does not reveal both inputs.

Seeing ā does not tell you whether it came from a + a, a + ā, ā + a or ā + ā. When reading backwards, use known words and meaning to recover the boundary. The sound rule alone cannot choose a unique split.
The joined devālaya is a compound stem. Its inflected forms belong in a later morphology lesson. Reverse sandhi proposes possibilities; vocabulary and grammar test them.

lessons.title: When a meets a different vowel
lessons.goal: Distinguish guṇa and vṛddhi outcomes without treating them as mere lengthening.
cards: The vowels are from different families. Instead of lengthening a or i, the boundary becomes e. Devendra is ‘lord of the gods’. The same e results when the first vowel is ā or the second is ī.
This vowel-sandhi outcome is called guṇa. Guṇa also appears in word formation for other grammatical reasons; not every e in Sanskrit proves this exact boundary.
Long ā does not change that answer.
Both inputs are long, but their combination is still e. Maheśvara means ‘great lord’. Decide by the vowel families, not by adding lengths or assuming that two long vowels must produce ai.
a+i, a+ī, ā+i and ā+ī all yield e in this ordinary setting. Morphological exceptions are a later lesson.

Hita means ‘beneficial’; upadeśa means ‘instruction’. At their boundary, a and u become o. The resulting expression means ‘beneficial instruction’. Any short/long combination of these two families has the ordinary result o.
The final visarga is already part of the supplied word form. This card changes only the vowel boundary.

Mahā means ‘great’, and ṛṣiḥ means ‘sage’. Their combination is maharṣiḥ. Notice ar: the preceding ā does not survive as ār in this ordinary compound. Prefixes before a root can follow a special rule.
Rare ḷ has the parallel theoretical result al after a/ā. We introduce the rare row for completeness, without giving it the same practice weight as common a/i/u combinations.

Sadā means ‘always’; eva adds emphasis. Their ā + e boundary becomes ai. A following ai also produces ai. Here the family of the second vowel leads to a different result from the previous i → e pattern.
This outcome is called vṛddhi sandhi. Compare a+i→e with a+e→ai; learning them as adjacent contrasts prevents confusion.
Jala is water; oghaḥ is a flood or mass. Their a + o boundary gives au. A following au gives the same boundary result. Jalaughaḥ means a flood or mass of water.
The two vṛddhi results are ai for e/ai and au for o/au. Do not interpret ai or au as two separately counted Sanskrit vowels.
a + i → e · i + a → ya
When a comes first, a + i gives e. When i comes first, it can become y before a. You cannot reverse the inputs and keep the same rule. The next lesson teaches that glide pattern.
These are sound demonstrations rather than vocabulary items. Label abstract rows clearly so learners do not mistake them for complete words.
अ / आ + इ · उ · ऋ · ए · ओ
When the first vowel is a or ā, identify the second family. i gives e; u gives o; ṛ gives ar; e or ai gives ai; o or au gives au. Like a vowels give ā, as you learned earlier.
This is the ordinary map. It applies after checking the setting and protection rules; a later card contrasts verbal augment and prefix exceptions.

lessons.title: A vowel becomes a glide
lessons.goal: Apply yaṇ with a dissimilar following vowel and preserve that vowel.
cards: Iti ends in i, while api begins in a. Because these are different vowel families, i becomes the glide y. The following a stays. The result is ityapi, roughly ‘thus also’, with its precise meaning supplied by context.
The traditional name is yaṇ sandhi. A glide is a consonantal sound related to a vowel; y is related to i.
Long ī can become y too.
Nadī means ‘river’; atra means ‘here’. Long ī changes to y before the dissimilar a. The following a still supplies the boundary vowel. The rule does not leave an extra ī syllable behind.
This is a teaching phrase: ‘the river [is] here’. Sanskrit can omit an explicit present-tense ‘is’. The glide rule treats both i and ī alike before a dissimilar vowel.

Su means ‘well’, and āgatam means ‘come’. At the u + ā boundary, u becomes v and ā remains. Svāgatam is the familiar ‘welcome’. Short u and long ū share this glide outcome before a different vowel family.
The ordinary y/v pronunciation must be learned from a competent Sanskrit speaker. This preview does not provide unverified synthetic pronunciation.

Pitṛ is the compound form ‘father’; ādeśaḥ means ‘instruction’. The vocalic ṛ becomes consonantal r before ā. The result means ‘a father’s instruction’. The following vowel supplies the syllable at the boundary.
ṝ has the same glide r. Rare ḷ has the corresponding glide l before a dissimilar vowel. Compound stems and standalone nominative word forms must not be interchanged.

The glide rule is not limited to a. Before e, final i becomes y and the e stays. Iti eva becomes ityeva, ‘just so / precisely thus’. Keep the second vowel rather than replacing it with the first vowel’s long form.
Before other dissimilar vowels, apply the same principle: i/ī→y, u/ū→v, ṛ/ṝ→r. The following vowel retains its identity under this step.

You already know this word. The two i vowels belong to the same family, so they merge into ī. The glide rule is for a dissimilar next vowel. Always compare the two families before replacing the first vowel.
Rare ṛ/ḷ combinations require their traditional savarṇa classification rather than treating them as ordinary dissimilar vowels. Use the reference for those cases.
A consonant is not a trigger.
The river flows: nadī vahati. The next word starts with consonant v, so the final ī does not become y. Seeing a familiar vowel ending is not enough; the next initial sound must satisfy the rule.
No change is a real result, not a missing rule. Independent words remain separate in this example even though continuous pronunciation links the phrase.
Recover the vowel through the glide.
y may point back to i or ī

When reading nadyatra, recognise atra and test nadī as the preceding word. The y can come from ī before a. A glide does not reveal the original vowel’s length, so vocabulary and grammar still complete the analysis.
Not every y or v comes from sandhi. Some are original consonants. Reverse analysis needs plausible words, not automatic replacement of every glide.

lessons.title: The special behaviour of e and o
lessons.goal: Distinguish internal ay/av from external elision and retained hiatus.
cards: Inside formations, e can open to ay.

In this schematic present-stem formation, e develops into ay before a: nayanti, ‘they lead’. This is an internal formation. Do not transfer its ay result automatically to independent words ending in e.
The diagram begins at an intermediate grammatical stage. It is not the full derivation from the root nī. Showing the stage keeps vowel sandhi separate from guṇa and tense formation.
The parallel for o is av.

The corresponding schematic formation gives bhavanti, ‘they are / become’. Before a vowel, internal o opens to av. The relation e→ay and o→av helps explain forms, but external boundaries need additional rules.
This begins after an earlier change from root bhū. Sandhi is one stage of derivation, not a replacement for the conjugation system. Internal ai→āy and au→āv follow the parallel pattern.
At a word boundary, short a disappears.
Te means ‘they’; api means ‘also’. The e stays and the initial short a drops. The mark ऽ, avagraha, records the lost a. Te’pi means ‘they too’. You do not pronounce the avagraha as a new sound.
This external rule also applies after ordinary final o: an initial short a is elided. Check pragṛhya status first, and distinguish lexical o from o arising through visarga sandhi.
Long ā does not disappear this way.
Te āgatāḥ means ‘they have come’. Here e changes to a, while the following long ā remains. Read the two boundary vowels separately. The short-a elision rule does not apply to a word beginning in ā.
The usual external ay loses its y in this setting. The resulting hiatus is normally retained. Do not run savarṇa-dīrgha again and collapse a + ā.
Other vowels keep the gap too.

Iha means ‘here’. Before its i, final e normally becomes a and leaves the following i intact. The result is ta iha, ‘they [are] here’. Two adjacent vowel syllables can therefore be correct in joined Sanskrit.

This retained hiatus follows loss of y. A space is helpful editorially, but the grammatical reason for the gap is the rule, not the space itself. Rare textual alternatives belong in detailed reference.
Tasyai means ‘to her’. Before a following vowel, external ai usually becomes ā. The next vowel remains separate: tasyā api, ‘to her too’. Do not combine the resulting ā and a a second time.
The internal corresponding outcome is āy. Grammarians allow retention in some descriptions, but loss of y and retained hiatus are the usual reading pattern in texts.

Tau means ‘those two’; eva adds emphasis. Here au becomes āv and the next e stays, giving tāveva. Unlike the usual external ai pattern, the v is retained. Learn this contrast rather than dropping every glide.
This is ordinary Classical usage. Older Vedic texts show additional variants; those require evidence from the particular text and its recitation tradition.
Ask whether o came from visarga.

The pause form rāmaḥ becomes rāma before iha, ‘here’. Do not invent an intermediate rāmo and apply a general o table to it. Start from the real word ending. Visarga sandhi will explain this family explicitly.

Lexical final o is uncommon and has exceptions: go in compounds, vocatives and certain particles need their own reference entries. The shared-looking surface o can conceal different grammatical histories.

lessons.title: When the ordinary vowel rule stops
lessons.goal: Recognise protected vowels and morphology-sensitive exceptions.
cards: Agnī here means ‘two fires’, and apaśyam means ‘I saw’. The dual ending ī remains before the next vowel: agnī apaśyam. This protected class is called pragṛhya. Identify the grammatical ending before applying the usual ī→y rule.
Dual ī, ū and e are the main pragṛhya endings. The final m in apaśyam is retained at a pause; if another consonant follows in continuous speech, final-m sandhi applies separately.

Bāhū means ‘two arms’; udyacchati means ‘raises’. The ū and following u remain separate. Do not merge them into ū simply because they are of one family. The dual ending’s protected status comes first.
This phrase means ‘[someone] raises two arms’. The same bāhu stem has other case and number endings; protection belongs to the specified dual forms, not to every word related to bāhu.
An e ending is not always protected.

Labhete is a dual verbal form: ‘the two obtain’. Its final e stays before aśvān, ‘horses’. Compare te + api → te’pi from the last lesson. Both end in e, but only the specified grammatical class receives protection.
Pragṛhya is not a spelling exception for every e. The learner needs number and form identification. The supplied aśvān is an accusative plural word form.

Amī means ‘those [men]’. Its ī is protected even though this form is plural, not dual. Certain particles and interjections also keep their vowels. These are named grammatical classes, so use a short exception list alongside the ordinary rules.

Whitney also lists final o produced with particle u, interjections such as aho, and Vedic protected pronominal or locative forms. These lexical and register-specific cases should have reference entries.
A prolonged vowel is a different case.
pluta: a vowel held for three mātrās

A specially prolonged vowel, often marked with ३, is not treated as an ordinary short or long vowel. Recognise it as a special speech setting. Do not turn ordinary ā + a into this prolonged vowel by adding their lengths.

Pluta occurs especially in calling, questioning and recitation contexts. Detailed accent and recitation rules belong in a dedicated phonetics or Vedic chapter. The displayed form is a notation demonstration, not a vocabulary word.
A prefix before ṛ can give ār.
With a verbal prefix ending in a or ā before a root beginning in ṛ, the result can be ār. This differs from mahā + ṛṣiḥ → maharṣiḥ. Identify prefix plus root before choosing the ordinary ar result.
This is a specialist formation, ‘approaches / reaches’. Dictionaries and grammatical analyses help identify the prefix and root; the surface sound pair alone is insufficient.
A prefix before e may keep only e.

Upetavya means ‘to be approached’. At this prefix boundary, a disappears and the following e remains. Ordinary a + e would give ai. This is a morphology-sensitive pattern, not permission to discard a at any word boundary.
Pararūpa patterns and lexical exceptions must be attached to the specific prefix/root or compound configuration. Whitney §137b includes upetavya, upetṛ and additional lexical examples.
A verbal augment can give vṛddhi.

The past-tense augment a is a grammatical element. In the cited formation, it gives ai before initial i, rather than the ordinary e. Corresponding u and ṛ cases can give au and ār. Identify the augment before applying the simple vowel table.
This is the grammatical example from Whitney §136a, rather than a free phrase ‘a + ita’. Teach its full tense formation in the verb chapter. Here it shows why sandhi needs grammatical context.

lessons.title: Final stops follow their neighbour
lessons.goal: Read voicing, nasalisation and dental assimilation at word boundaries.
cards: Begin with a valid word ending.
Form the word before joining it

Vāc is the stem ‘speech’; its pause form is vāk. External sandhi starts from the appropriate word form, not a raw dictionary stem. Learn the supplied forms with their morphology so that you do not apply a joining rule to the wrong input.

Usual final consonants are k, ṭ, t, p, ṅ, n, m and ḥ; rare ṇ and l occur too. Cluster reduction and stem-specific finals have exceptions, so ‘every palatal becomes k’ is not a complete derivation rule.
Voiced neighbours voice a final stop.

Tat means ‘that’; asti means ‘exists / is’. A vowel is voiced, so final t becomes d. Tadasti means ‘that exists’. The vowel itself stays. This is consonant sandhi even though the next word begins with a vowel.
The ordinary final-stop correspondences are k→g, ṭ→ḍ, t→d and p→b before voiced sounds. Pause forms and connected forms differ.

G is a voiced stop. Final t therefore becomes d before gacchati, ‘goes’. The result is tadgacchati, ‘that goes’. You are changing voicing, not moving the dental t to the g sound’s place of articulation.
Voicing and place are separate checks. Final t has extra place-assimilation rules before palatal and retroflex sounds; the next cards add those.
An unvoiced neighbour keeps it unvoiced.
Ph is unvoiced, even though it is aspirated. Final t stays t. Tat phalam means ‘that fruit’. A following h inside the Roman symbol ph does not make ph two consonants or turn it into voiced h.
Aspirated kh, ch, ṭh, th and ph are unvoiced stops. Gh, jh, ḍh, dh and bh are voiced. The independent consonant h behaves differently.
Before a nasal, a nasal result is possible.

Na means ‘not’. A common joined form is tanna: the dental t becomes dental n before the nasal. Other final stops can similarly become their own class’s nasal. This nasal assimilation is an allowed alternative to simple voicing.

The voiced alternative tad na is also permitted in grammatical descriptions. Class nasals are ṅ for k, ṇ for ṭ, n for t and m for p. Mark optionality rather than treating one spelling as the only correct output.
Before c or j, t changes its place.
tat citram → taccitram · tat jalam → tajjalam

Citram means ‘picture’; jalam means ‘water’. Before these palatal stops, final t becomes a palatal stop too. It remains unvoiced before c and becomes voiced before j. The double consonants represent two consonantal positions.
The same place pattern applies before ch and jh. Compare voiced and unvoiced rows; teach the shared cause instead of presenting four unrelated answers.
Retroflex stops have their own row.
t + ṭ → ṭṭ · t + ḍ → ḍḍ

Before a retroflex stop, final dental t changes to the retroflex place. Voicing follows the neighbour: ṭ before ṭ, ḍ before ḍ. These sound demonstrations extend the same place-and-voice reasoning to the retroflex row.
This is an abstract boundary demonstration, not a sentence. Before ṭh and ḍh the corresponding first result is ṭ and ḍ. Do not apply this row to every consonant pronounced nearby, such as ṣ.
Before l, t can become l.
Labhasva means ‘obtain’. Final t assimilates to the following l, producing two l sounds: tallabhasva, ‘obtain that’. Keep this row distinct from merely voicing t to d.
The written double ll is a genuine cluster across the old boundary. It is not the same as a single long vowel or an extra syllable.
The next word can change too.

Hi is an emphatic particle. One common joined form is taddhi: final t voices to d, and h becomes the matching aspirated dh. Sandhi may alter both sides of a boundary, rather than only the last letter of the first word.

Retention of h with a voiced first stop is also allowed: tad hi. Parallel common forms are k+h→g+gh, ṭ+h→ḍ+ḍh and p+h→b+bh. A human pronunciation recording would make the aspiration contrast easier to hear.

Śivam here means ‘auspicious’. A common result is tacchivam: t becomes c and the following ś becomes ch. Read c + ch as a cluster. This is different from the single aspirated consonant ch you met earlier.

The ś→ch substitution has grammatical conditions and variants, especially when ś itself begins a cluster. The retained-ś form is encountered too; do not extrapolate this simple example to all ś sequences.

lessons.title: Nasals and small inserted sounds
lessons.goal: Distinguish m, n, anusvāra and nasal consonant variants.
cards: Final m becomes anusvāra before a consonant.

Vanam means ‘to the forest’ here; gacchati means ‘goes’. Final m is written as anusvāra before g: vanaṃ gacchati. This explains a very frequent dot in connected Sanskrit. It is not an ordinary vowel mark.
Anusvāra pronunciation depends on the following sound and the reading tradition. A visual dot is not a universal instruction to pronounce an isolated m in every environment.
Before a vowel, m remains m.
Phalam means ‘fruit’. Before the vowel a in asti, final m stays m: phalamasti, ‘there is a fruit’. Contrast this with m before a consonant. At a pause, the ordinary final m is retained too.
The m may be written attached to the next vowel in continuous Devanagari. Its changed appearance as म does not mean it acquired a new vowel of its own.
A dot can correspond to a class nasal.

Khādāmi means ‘I eat’. Before kh, the nasal may be represented by anusvāra or by the matching velar nasal ṅ. These are permitted connected forms. The specific nasal has the same mouth position as the following stop.

The five stop-class nasals are ṅ, ñ, ṇ, n and m. Modern editions often prefer anusvāra notation. Semivowel and h contexts have further phonetic conventions; do not assume every dot has the same realisation.
Final n matches a following voiced palatal.
Tān means ‘them’; jayati means ‘conquers’. The dental n becomes palatal ñ before j. Before voiced retroflex ḍ or ḍh, the matching nasal is ṇ. Class and voicing help you recognise the result.
Do not apply this nasal-place rule to k or g at an ordinary word boundary: final n is not automatically replaced before every stop. The retroflex combinations are rare in real vocabulary.
Before an unvoiced stop, a sibilant appears.

Ca means ‘and’. The n ending before c gives anusvāra plus ś: tāṃśca, ‘and them’. This is more than nasal place matching. Remember the inserted sibilant so that you can recover the original n ending when reading.

Historically many final n forms continue older ns. The Classical pattern extends beyond those historical originals. It is useful to recognise the mechanism without requiring historical linguistics before reading.
The dental and retroflex rows parallel it.
Tarati means ‘crosses’. Before t, final n gives anusvāra plus dental s. Before retroflex ṭ, the added sibilant is ṣ. Learn the three unvoiced rows together: c gets ś, ṭ gets ṣ, and t gets s.
The ṭ row is shown as an abstract sound combination because common vocabulary examples are sparse. Aspirated ch, ṭh and th follow their respective rows too.
n before l produces a nasal l.
Labhate means ‘obtains’. Before l, final n may be written as a nasalised l followed by l. The small nasal sign matters: this is not simply the plain ll from tat + labhasva.

Editions differ in writing nasal l: anusvāra, chandrabindu and explicit nasalised-consonant spellings occur. Preserve the edition’s notation and teach its pronunciation rather than marking every alternative wrong.
Before ś, ñ and ch may appear.

Śocati means ‘mourns’. One form retains ś after ñ; another changes ś to ch. Both reveal an original n ending. A reader needs to recognise the permitted alternatives instead of memorising one joined spelling as the only possible form.

The change of ś has conditions when another consonant follows it. Before s or ṣ, n normally remains n; optional transitional t is recorded, as in mahān san / mahānt san. These are separate rows, not the n+c rule.
A short vowel before n can cause doubling.
Short vowel + final n + vowel → nn

Gacchan means ‘going’. Its final n follows short a and meets the next vowel, so it doubles: gacchannasti, ‘[he] is going’. Both conditions matter: the preceding vowel is short and the next sound is a vowel.

Final ṅ has a parallel doubling rule after a short vowel before a vowel. Final n after a long vowel does not double by this rule: tān + api → tānapi. Some grammatical accounts include rare ṇ contexts.
ch after a short vowel gains c.

Atra means ‘here’; chāyā means ‘shade’. Short a before ch causes an added c: atracchāyā, ‘there is shade here’. This explains another double-looking cluster. The original ch remains one aspirated consonant, preceded by an extra c.

After most long vowels this insertion is optional; after the specified particles ā and mā it is prescribed. The full tug-āgama conditions belong in reference. Do not derive every cch solely from this one environment.

lessons.title: The common aḥ and āḥ endings
lessons.goal: Distinguish four common visarga environments and keep resulting hiatus.
cards: The preceding vowel changes the rule.

Rāmaḥ is a singular form; rāmāḥ is plural. Before voiced sounds, these two endings behave differently. Read the vowel before visarga carefully. A table that says only ‘ḥ changes’ hides the information needed to choose the result.
These ordinary nominal endings continue -as and -ās. Underlying r-final words need different treatment even when their pause spelling also contains visarga.
aḥ becomes o before a voiced consonant.

Rama goes: rāmo gacchati. The ordinary aḥ ending becomes o before voiced g. Other voiced consonants have the same basic outcome. The next word remains intact; only the first word’s ending changes here.
Voiced sounds include voiced stops, nasals, semivowels and h. Specific pronouns saḥ and eṣaḥ are exceptions introduced later.
Before short a, keep o and omit a.

Now the opening example makes sense. Ordinary aḥ before short a gives o, and the following a is elided. Avagraha marks that lost a: rāmo’sti, ‘Rama is here / exists’. It adds no syllable and is not a pause sign.
The same visible o’ also occurs after lexical e/o plus short a. To reverse it, use the word form and context, rather than assuming every apostrophe proves aḥ.
Iha means ‘here’. The aḥ ending becomes a before i, while i remains. Read rāma iha, with two boundary vowels. Do not change it into rāmeha by applying a + i sandhi again.
The hiatus created by visarga loss is retained in ordinary Classical usage. The rule covers following vowels other than short a, including long ā.

Āgacchati means ‘comes’. Because its initial vowel is long ā, the short-a elision pattern does not apply. The visarga disappears and the two vowels remain: rāma āgacchati. The length mark is essential to choosing the rule.
This resulting a + ā must not be merged again by savarṇa-dīrgha. Similar-looking adjacent vowels can arise from different grammatical histories.
āḥ loses visarga before a voiced consonant.

The Ramas go: rāmā gacchanti. Long ā remains and visarga disappears. It does not become o. Compare the singular rāmo gacchati with this plural form; the grammatical ending and verb number support your reading.
The name is used here as a countable plural to contrast endings. Ordinary nouns such as narāḥ ‘men’ show the same -ās-origin pattern.
āḥ leaves a gap before vowels.

Bālāḥ means ‘children’; api means ‘also’. Ordinary āḥ loses its visarga, but the following a remains separate. Do not merge the two vowels into bālāpi. This is another correct hiatus created by visarga sandhi.
The rule presupposes an -ās-origin ending. A rare āḥ pause form from underlying ār, such as dvāḥ, behaves differently before voiced sounds.
Unvoiced stops do not use the o rule.
Rama reads: rāmaḥ paṭhati. P is unvoiced, so the ordinary aḥ→o rule does not apply. Before k, kh, p and ph, visarga is normally retained in writing. The next lesson handles the other unvoiced rows.
Before k/kh and p/ph, specialised recitation can use jihvāmūlīya and upadhmānīya allophones. Their exact articulation and symbols need an expert phonetics lesson, not a guessed recording.

lessons.title: Visarga beyond aḥ
lessons.goal: Recognise sibilants, r outcomes, r collision and pronoun exceptions.
cards: Before c, visarga can become ś.

Bālaḥ means ‘the boy’; carati means ‘walks’. Visarga becomes the palatal sibilant ś before c. The joined bālaścarati means ‘the boy walks’. This is a place-matching result, unlike the o before voiced g.

The ordinary row applies to simple following c/ch environments. Clusters that begin with these sounds can have additional qualifications; consult the detailed reference when a second consonant follows immediately.
Before t, the sibilant is s.

Tiṣṭhati means ‘stands’. Before dental t, visarga becomes dental s: bālastiṣṭhati, ‘the boy stands’. Before a retroflex ṭ or ṭh, the corresponding sibilant is ṣ. Match the sibilant to the following stop’s class.
The compact IAST reading is bālastiṣṭhati. The retroflex row is ḥ+ṭ→ṣṭ, not a general conversion of visarga to ṣ everywhere.
Before a sibilant, editions can differ.
ḥ before ś / ṣ / s · alternatives

Śete means ‘lies down’. Visarga may be retained, or assimilated to the following sibilant. Both rāmaḥ śete and rāmaś śete occur as permitted representations. The corresponding ṣ and s contexts have parallel alternatives.

A following cluster may favour or require retention under detailed rules. Teach one normal reading, then show permitted variants with their environments. Avoid treating an edition’s spelling preference as a different meaning.
After i or u, voiced sounds give r.

Agniḥ means ‘fire’. Before voiced a, its ending becomes ir: agnirasti, ‘there is fire’. Vāyuḥ + asti similarly gives vāyurasti, ‘there is wind’. These endings do not follow the ordinary short-aḥ→o pattern.
Outside the -as/-ās cases, s-origin and r-origin visarga generally give r before voiced sounds. Unvoiced following sounds still use the visarga/sibilant rules.
Two r sounds are not kept together.
Punaḥ comes from punar, ‘again’. Before ramate, ‘enjoys’, the meeting r is lost and the preceding a lengthens: punā ramate. After i or u, the corresponding collision can give ī or ū.
Examples include agniḥ + rocate → agnī rocate and vāyuḥ + rocate → vāyū rocate. Ordinary -as-origin aḥ before r instead follows the o pattern, as rāmaḥ + ramate → rāmo ramate.
A pause form can hide an original r.
Underlying punar → r before voiced sound

Punaḥ is ‘again’. Before api, its underlying r returns: punarapi, ‘again also’. Do not use the aḥ + a → o’ rule here. The familiar pause spelling alone does not distinguish s-origin from r-origin visarga.
The rare door form dvāḥ continues dvār and gives dvār before voiced sounds, rather than the ordinary -ās loss rule. Keep lexical origin in the content model and reference entry.
saḥ has a special consonant rule.
saḥ / eṣaḥ · drop ḥ before consonants
Saḥ means ‘he / that one’. Before a consonant, its visarga drops: sa gacchati, ‘he goes’. It does not become so gacchati. Eṣaḥ, ‘this one’, follows the same special pattern.
Before vowels other than short a, these pronouns also lose visarga and retain hiatus. At a pause, use saḥ and eṣaḥ. Treat these as named lexical exceptions, not a new general rule for all aḥ endings.
Before short a, saḥ uses so’.
The pronoun’s short-a case follows the familiar o’ outcome: so’sti, ‘he is here / exists’. Eṣaḥ + asti gives eṣo’sti. Pair this with sa gacchati so that the exception is learned with its own limits.
Optional behaviours in metrical or older texts require separate evidence. The main path teaches the ordinary Classical prose patterns before introducing those register-specific alternatives.

lessons.title: Changes inside a formed word
lessons.goal: See why internal consonant sandhi needs roots and endings, not just a word-boundary chart.
cards: Do not voice every internal consonant.

Vacmi means ‘I speak’. The c remains before voiced m in this internal formation. External final-stop voicing is not a universal rule for every adjacent pair inside words. Identify the root and the ending first.

The root vac belongs to a conjugational system. This example teaches a sound outcome, not the entire paradigm. Internal vowels, nasals and semivowels generally do not have the same voicing effect as in external sandhi.
Some case endings behave like pada boundaries.

Now revisit ‘by the winds’. Before case ending bhiḥ, final t voices to d. Internal formation does sometimes resemble external joining. Learn which endings receive that treatment rather than declaring all internal and external rules identical.
Endings beginning with bh and s are traditionally important pada endings, including bhyām, bhiḥ, bhyaḥ and su. Detailed stem classes belong with declension.
Aspiration can move to the next stop.

The formation budh + ta gives buddha, ‘awakened’. The first stop loses its aspiration, while the following stop becomes dh. The resulting cluster is d + dh. Its Roman ddh is not three independent consonants.
This is a root-plus-suffix demonstration. Consonant adjustment and preservation of aspiration work together; the full participle derivation is a morphology lesson.
Another root shows the same mechanism.

Labh + ta gives labdha, ‘obtained’. The labial first stop becomes unaspirated b; the dental second stop becomes dh. Compare buddha: aspiration is preserved, but the first stop’s place is supplied by its own root.
Do not derive labdha by changing every consonant to the same mouth position. Aspiration, place and voicing are different features.
Aspiration may return to an earlier consonant.
Aspiration shifts back in this root

In the cited formation, aspiration cannot stay on the final stop before s, so it appears on the root’s initial b: bhotsya. The result is a future-stem stage. This is a root-sensitive process, not an instruction to aspirate any earlier letter.
Whitney treats aspiration transfer in a specified class of roots. Keep the root and derivational stage in the data. A surface-only sandhi table cannot supply this information.

The root dah means ‘burn’. In this future-stem formation, the result is dhakṣya. The h does not simply become one fixed consonant in every environment. Study h-final roots through their attested forms and grammatical class.
Do not present this as the complete finite verb; the appropriate personal ending follows. Other h-final roots may have different outcomes, so dictionary and morphology support are required.
A preceding ṣ can make t retroflex.

Dviṣ means ‘hate’. Before the suffix ta, the dental t becomes retroflex ṭ after ṣ, giving dviṣṭa, ‘hated’. Here the second member changes to match a preceding sound. Sandhi effects can work in either direction.
Some palatal roots also show ṣṭ, kṣ or other outcomes under specified formations. Root-final c, j, ś and h require morphological classes, not one universal conversion rule.
Read the finished form, then inspect its history.

When you meet labdha, recognise ‘obtained’. Then inspect labh + ta and explain b + dh. This connects sandhi to useful vocabulary. Learning isolated transformations without the root, ending and meaning would leave you unable to recognise the word in a text.
Internal sandhi is revisited throughout nouns, verbs and compounds. This chapter establishes the mechanisms; each morphology chapter must teach its own relevant formations and exceptions.

lessons.title: When s and n become retroflex
lessons.goal: Apply ṣatva and ṇatva with their triggers, blockers and word limits.
cards: After i, s can become ṣ.

Agni + su forms agniṣu, ‘in fires’. The suffix’s dental s becomes retroflex ṣ after i. This is an internal formation. It does not mean that every word starting in s changes after any preceding word ending in i.
Ṣatva applies under specified internal, prefix and compound conditions. IAST s, ś and ṣ represent three different consonants; do not collapse them into one English s.
The trigger set is larger than i.

Dhanus means ‘bow’. In dhanuṣā, ‘with a bow’, the s after u becomes ṣ. Triggering sounds include the i and u vowel groups, vocalic ṛ, and k or r under the specified conditions. The nickname ‘ruki’ helps remember this family.
The expanded vowel set includes ī, ū, ṝ, e, ai, o and au. A trigger is not sufficient in every lexical configuration: check morphology and exceptions.
A following r can block ṣatva.
i before s · but sr remains

Tisraḥ is a feminine form of ‘three’. Despite the preceding i, the s remains dental before r. This is a useful counterexample to ‘i always changes s to ṣ’. The following sounds matter as well as the previous one.
Whitney §181 discusses the following-r restriction and root-sensitive exceptions. Teach this visible counterexample in the main path; reserve the extensive lexical list for reference.
r can turn a later n into ṇ.
rāmena → rāmeṇa, showing the nasal step
Rāmeṇa means ‘by / with Rama’. The r earlier in the word triggers a retroflex ṇ in the ending. The sounds need not be adjacent. First locate the trigger, then inspect what comes between it and n.
The left side schematically isolates the final nasal step after the case-ending formation. It is not a standalone Sanskrit word rāmena or the full derivation of the instrumental ending.
Some sounds allow that influence through.
Vowels and labials do not block here

In rāmeṇa, m and e lie between r and n. They do not block this ṇatva change. Vowels, y, v, gutturals and labials commonly allow the influence through. In the appropriate formation, earlier r, ṛ, ṝ or ṣ can trigger it.

The traditional rule also specifies what follows the affected n. In the ordinary internal rule, it is followed by a vowel, n, m, y or v. Final n is not automatically retroflexed just because an earlier r exists.
A dental can stop the influence.
th between r and n · blocked

Rathena means ‘by / with a chariot’. The dental th intervenes between r and the ending’s n. The n stays dental. Compare rāmeṇa, where the intervening m did not block the change. This contrast gives the rule a clear boundary.
Palatal, retroflex and dental consonants generally block the preceding influence; y is an important allowed exception. Prefix and compound configurations have further conditions.
Ordinary separate words have a limit.
External r | n · n remains n

Hari bows: harirnamati. Visarga becomes r before n, but that external r does not automatically turn the next word’s n into ṇ. Keep the normal word boundary limit. Internal retroflexion is not a free rule across every Classical sentence.

Certain compounds, prefixes and Vedic combinations extend these processes under particular rules. Learn those as named formations, rather than erasing the distinction between independent words and one integral word.
A good explanation includes a blocker.

To explain ṇ, name the trigger, show the intervening sounds, and confirm the grammatical setting. To explain dental n, show what blocked the change or why the setting does not allow it. This gives more depth than memorising which words happen to contain ṇ.
Detailed exceptions must be revisited with compounds, prefixes and paradigms. This chapter teaches the productive reasoning, while the source reference supports forms outside the common pattern.

lessons.title: Read a whole passage
lessons.goal: Reconnect rule families, recover words and test ambiguous splits against meaning.
cards: रामः इह अस्ति । सः अपि वनम् गच्छति ।

‘Rama is here. He too goes to the forest.’ Read the two short sentences as a whole first. Next we will inspect one boundary per card while keeping this passage visible. The aim is to understand connected Sanskrit, not just fill a sandhi table.
This is an original teaching passage, not a quotation from a scripture. The separate-word line exposes grammatical word forms; it does not show the final continuous pronunciation.
रामः इह अस्ति । सः अपि वनम् गच्छति ।
Rāmaḥ meets iha. Ordinary aḥ before a vowel other than short a loses visarga and leaves a. The initial i remains. Keep this boundary gap; do not merge rāma and iha into rāmeha.
The displayed passage stays anchored so the learner can locate the current change. A production version can underline whole shaped sound spans without splitting a Devanagari conjunct.
रामः इह अस्ति । सः अपि वनम् गच्छति ।

This is a different boundary. Final a of iha meets initial a of asti, so the ordinary like-vowel rule gives ā. Ihāsti means ‘is here’. The retained gap before iha does not forbid a valid change at the next original boundary.
Apply rules to the original relevant boundaries, not blindly to every new adjacent pair created by a deletion. This distinction prevents both over-joining and under-joining.
रामः इह अस्ति । सः अपि वनम् गच्छति ।
The second sentence begins so’pi. Recover saḥ, ‘he’, and api, ‘also’. The following vowel is short a, so this pronoun uses o’ here. Its exception before consonants would give sa, as in sa gacchati.
The pronoun refers back to Rama. Grammar and discourse support this split; the visible o’ mark alone does not identify which word came before it.
रामः इह अस्ति । सः अपि वनम् गच्छति ।

Vanaṃ before gacchati comes from vanam, ‘to the forest’. Final m changes to anusvāra before a consonant. Restoring the word ending lets you recognise its grammatical function and understand where the person is going.
The reading has no hidden extra example. Keep the same sentence visible while explaining the nasal, then reassemble it with all the earlier changes.
Put meaning and sound back together.
रामः इह अस्ति । सः अपि वनम् गच्छति ।

Read it again with meaning: ‘Rama is here. He too goes to the forest.’ You can now explain visarga loss, like-vowel merger, the pronoun’s o’ form, and anusvāra. Each small rule has a place in one coherent reading.
Reading progress means you have seen the explanation. A later check should ask you to explain fresh boundaries and recover words without the separated line. Do not label this reading step as mastery.
Reverse sandhi can have more than one answer.
deva + indra or devā + indra → devendra

The e result can arise from different short/long inputs. Not every formally possible split produces sensible vocabulary and grammar. Use a dictionary, word forms and sentence meaning to choose a plausible analysis; do not let a reverse-sandhi tool choose blindly.
The alternatives here are schematic vowel-boundary candidates, not equally established interpretations of the compound devendra. In genuine reading, ambiguity may require several grammatical parses.
Carry a procedure, not a hundred answers.

Find the boundary sounds. Check the ending, word form and setting. Apply the appropriate family rule, including its exceptions. Then test the recovered words against meaning. You now have the common Classical map; return to each rule when it appears in nouns, verbs and real reading.

Next learning steps: fresh-text explanation checks, spaced review of confusable cases, compound-specific exceptions, and internal formations within morphology. Vedic accent, recitation variants and exhaustive Pāṇinian rule ordering are separate advanced strands.
